problem_motivation.content: Explaining why wet-chemical growth does not yield h-CuI on open monolayer graphene
problem_motivation.evidence_span: it offers an explanation for the absence of h-CuI on open monolayer regions in the wet-chemical route [26].

prior_approach.content: Prior simulations studied freestanding and encapsulated 2D h-CuI, but not open-substrate supported h-CuI
prior_approach.evidence_span: Published calculations thus considered the freestanding monolayer [17,23] and the encapsulated layer [26,28] but not yet 2D h-CuI on an open graphene substrate

prior_approach.content: Prior work by Ullah et al. computed registry-dependent stacking energy by sliding and rotating encapsulated CuI/graphene across five configurations
prior_approach.evidence_span: The upper bound of this range is derived from Ullah et al. [S11], who computed the registry-dependent stacking energy of CuI encapsulated by graphene by sliding and rotating the layers across five distinct configurations and found the total energy variation to be < 0.3 meV/atom

rejected_alternative.content: γ-CuI growth route is excluded because it requires high-temperature CuI vapor flux absent here
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: routes that yield γ-CuI nanosheets and epitaxial γ-CuI films sublime CuI powder from sources held at 360–450 °C [24,25]; in our process no component exceeds 180 °C, far below appreciable CuI sublimation, so the molecular CuI flux that enables γ-phase growth is absent.

rejected_alternative.content: Multilayer h-CuI/β-CuI formation is considered unlikely because basal planes are self-saturating and precursors are supplied on graphene, not atop h-CuI
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Second, the h-CuI surface is self-saturating: its basal planes carry no dangling bonds, so the iodine-terminated basal h-CuI plane cannot template γ-CuI. Moreover, the precursor species Cu and I are supplied on graphene and not on top of h-CuI, so a second layer cannot nucleate, which makes multilayer h-CuI (β-CuI) equally unlikely.

inspiration_source.content: Film compression/deposition method is modeled after the Langmuir–Blodgett process
inspiration_source.evidence_span: The compression was analogous to the Langmuir–Blodgett process, with the difference that the SDS molecules rearranged by self-assembly, so that a compact, uniform monolayer was maintained throughout the deposition.

causal_claim.content: HI vapor both reduces oxo-G and etches the copper grid, providing Cu source
causal_claim.evidence_span: where HI serves a dual purpose: it reduces the oxo-G to reduced oxo-graphene (r-oxo-G) [30], and it attacks the copper of the grid, the solid-state copper source of the synthesis.

causal_claim.content: Annealing at 180 °C grows initial crystallites into extended vdW-epitaxial domains
causal_claim.evidence_span: In the second step, annealing at 180 °C grows the crystallites into extended, van der Waals-epitaxial domains.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing improves crystallinity and enables lattice relaxation
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thermal annealing at 180 °C significantly improves crystallinity and promotes lattice relaxation.

causal_claim.content: Annealing promotes further growth of intercalated bilayer domains
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thermal annealing at 180 °C promotes the further growth of these intercalated domains [Fig. 4(d)].

causal_claim.content: Growth in bilayer proceeds analogously to open monolayer growth
causal_claim.evidence_span: In both, h-CuI grows epitaxially with a hexagonal lattice, which shows that intercalation into twisted bilayer graphene proceeds analogously to growth on the open monolayer surface.

causal_claim.content: Annealing reduces oxygen signal, indicating removal of oxygen groups and adsorbed water
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thermal annealing significantly reduces the oxygen signal in the EDX maps (see Fig. S1e), indicating the effective removal of oxygen-containing functional groups and adsorbed water from the initial oxo-G template during the HI treatment and subsequent annealing.

causal_claim.content: Separate precursor arrival at graphene makes local supersaturation for 3D γ-CuI nucleation unlikely
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thus, CuI forms in situ under dilute conditions, and the local supersaturation required to nucleate a three-dimensional γ-CuI particle is unlikely to be reached.

causal_claim.content: Interfacial adlayers strongly weaken adhesion
causal_claim.evidence_span: In contrast, interfacial adlayers have a pronounced effect on the epitaxial growth.

causal_claim.content: Remaining adsorbates suppress adhesion recovery and halt growth
causal_claim.evidence_span: where adsorbates remain on the surface, the adhesion term of Eq. (1) is not recovered and growth stops.

causal_claim.content: Single-layer graphene damps relative out-of-plane h-CuI motion by about an order of magnitude
causal_claim.evidence_span: Thus, a single graphene layer damps the relative out-of-plane movement of h-CuI between 1.20 and 1.55 THz by an order of magnitude in normalized power.

causal_claim.content: A second graphene interface stiffens the in-plane transverse optical mode
causal_claim.evidence_span: For this collective in-plane movement, a second interface stiffens the h-CuI sheet.

causal_claim.content: HI vapor both reduces oxo-graphene and initiates nucleation of small h-CuI crystallites using iodine from HI and copper from the TEM grid
causal_claim.evidence_span: This treatment reduces the oxo-G and simultaneously initiates the nucleation of small h-CuI crystallites, formed from iodine supplied by the reducing agent and copper provided by the TEM grid.

causal_claim.content: Annealing at 180 °C promotes iodine-copper reaction to form extended, well-defined h-CuI crystals on or between reduced oxo-graphene sheets
causal_claim.evidence_span: Finally, the sample undergoes thermal annealing at 180 °C, which promotes the reaction between iodine and copper to form extended, well-defined h-CuI crystals on the reduced oxo-G (r-oxo-G) substrate or sandwiched between the graphene nanosheets of bilayer r-oxo-G.

causal_claim.content: Absence of h-CuI on Au confirms Cu grid is the only Cu source in the synthesis
causal_claim.evidence_span: The absence of h-CuI formation on the Au grid confirms that the copper from the Cu TEM grid is the sole source of Cu atoms in our synthesis, validating the solid-state precursor approach.

causal_claim.content: Stiffer graphene suppresses lateral relaxation of soft h-CuI, making the laterally constrained uniaxial estimate applicable
causal_claim.evidence_span: This laterally constrained form (εyy ≈ 0) is the upper estimate of the uniaxial strain cost, applicable when the stiffer graphene substrate (E2DGr ≈ 340 N/m) suppresses lateral relaxation of the soft h-CuI (E2D ≈ 35 N/m, Table S3).

causal_claim.content: An interfacial adlayer strongly reduces van der Waals stabilization needed for supported h-CuI growth
causal_claim.evidence_span: Such an interfacial layer therefore strongly reduces the van der Waals stabilization required for growth of supported h-CuI.

causal_claim.content: Supported h-CuI follows graphene out-of-plane motion more closely than encapsulated h-CuI pairs
causal_claim.evidence_span: The supported h-CuI sheet follows the out-of-plane motion of its graphene layer more closely than either pair of the encapsulated cell.

mechanism_principle.content: Cu released from the grid diffuses over graphene and reacts with adsorbed iodine to nucleate h-CuI
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The copper released from the grid crosses the graphene by surface diffusion, on a potential energy landscape flat enough for copper adatoms to migrate anomalously at room temperature [32], and meets the iodine adsorbed during the HI treatment, where small hexagonal CuI (h-CuI) crystallites nucleate.

mechanism_principle.content: Preferred 30° epitaxial offset arises because iodine occupies graphene hexagon centers
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Physically, the 30° offset reflects the energetically preferred registry in which the iodine atoms occupy the centers of the graphene hexagons [26]; this hexagon-center sublattice is rotated by 30° relative to the graphene atomic lattice, so θ = 0 corresponds to perfect epitaxial lock-in (Section S2c).

mechanism_principle.content: Near-isotropy of small bilayer nuclei is attributed to early growth stage and high edge-to-area ratio
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: We attribute the near-absence of in-plane anisotropy to the early stage of growth: the nucleus is small and has a high edge-to-area ratio, so its lattice has not yet developed the directional adaptation that characterizes larger, fully grown domains.

mechanism_principle.content: Registry with different graphene layers proves h-CuI is encapsulated rather than on outer bilayer surface
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: A crystallite on an outer surface of bilayer graphene would be templated by the outermost sheet in both cases, so registry with different graphene layers would be impossible. Both crystals are shown together in one image in Fig. S2, identifying the h-CuI as encapsulated within two graphene sheets (Section S3).

mechanism_principle.content: Hexagonal phase need not be thermodynamically preferred because γ-CuI nucleation conditions never occur
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Under these conditions where HI functions as both the reducing agent and the iodine source, the hexagonal phase does not have to be thermodynamically more favorable than γ-CuI. The conditions under which γ-CuI nucleates do not arise in the first place.

mechanism_principle.content: Prior DFT underestimation is ascribed to simplified vdW potential
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: which we ascribe to the unavoidable simplification in the vdW potential assumed in those calculations.

mechanism_principle.content: Such reduced adhesion cannot offset the metastability penalty of 2D h-CuI relative to γ-CuI
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: which cannot compensate the 20.5 meV/Å2 by which the 2D phase lies above bulk γ-CuI.

mechanism_principle.content: In bilayers, vdW pressure expels adsorbates and presses layers together, improving binding
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Within a bilayer, the van der Waals pressure expels part of the adsorbates into pockets [42,43] and presses the layers together, supporting the binding where adsorbates cannot be removed.

mechanism_principle.content: Residual oxo-groups, water, and iodine after 40 °C treatment limit crystal size
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: After the 40 °C HI treatment the reduced oxo-graphene surface still carries residual oxo-groups, physisorbed water, and adsorbed iodine [35], limiting the size of the h-CuI crystallites.

mechanism_principle.content: Larger domain size correlates with adsorbate removal and local interface cleanliness
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This correlation is consistent with a contribution from adsorbate removal; ... The lateral domain size therefore correlates with the local cleanliness of the interface, as seen in Fig. S2, where the h-CuI crystals extend up to the next adsorbate on the surface.

mechanism_principle.content: Graphene’s vdW spring damps nearby iodine sublayer out-of-plane motion
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The vdW spring of graphene thus damps the out-of-plane movement of the iodine sublayer in its vicinity.

mechanism_principle.content: Large strain anisotropy explains preference for uniaxial adaptation
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This anisotropy factor [Eq. (S8)] helps explain the preference for uniaxial adaptation observed experimentally.

mechanism_principle.content: Adhesion decreases steeply with increased gap because of the z^-4 tail of the planar vdW potential
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The adhesion decays steeply due to the z −4 tail.

hypothesis_statement.content: Oxo-G retains sufficient lattice periodicity to template vdW epitaxy
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: These well-defined crystallographic signatures demonstrate that the oxo-G retains the lattice periodicity required to act as a robust template for van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy.

hypothesis_statement.content: Formation-energy estimates indicate h-CuI is metastable
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: An estimate of the formation energies indicates that h-CuI is metastable.

evidence_result.content: Control on gold grids produced no h-CuI, showing Cu comes from the copper grid
evidence_result.evidence_span: The copper originates solely from the grid: a control synthesis on a gold (Au) TEM grid, under otherwise identical conditions, yields no h-CuI (Supporting Information, Section S1).

evidence_result.content: HI treatment alone produces ~5 nm h-CuI nuclei on mono- and bilayer graphene
evidence_result.evidence_span: HRTEM imaging revealed the nucleation of discrete h-CuI crystallites of about 5 nm on monolayer and bilayer r-oxo-G.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, domains are larger and diffraction sharper
evidence_result.evidence_span: Post-annealing HRTEM imaging [Fig. 3(d)] reveals increased domain sizes and sharper diffraction spots [Fig. 3(e)]

evidence_result.content: h-CuI adapts to graphene uniaxially, with one direction commensurate and the perpendicular near intrinsic spacing
evidence_result.evidence_span: The adaptation is uniaxial: along one direction an h-CuI vector matches the substrate period, while the perpendicular vector stays close to the intrinsic h-CuI value and retains a residual mismatch of about 1.4% (from the initial 1.67% lattice mismatch).

evidence_result.content: Bilayer-intercalated early nuclei are nearly isotropic
evidence_result.evidence_span: These values correspond to an essentially isotropic crystallite.

evidence_result.content: Annealed bilayer h-CuI shows 1.7% anisotropy with one direction relaxed near intrinsic spacing
evidence_result.evidence_span: The anisotropy of 1.7% indicates the uniaxial strain profile, reflecting the lattice adaptation to the epitaxial template in only one direction, while h-CuI remains relaxed in the perpendicular direction, where b1 = 0.419 ± 0.002 nm is close to the intrinsic value.

evidence_result.content: EDX shows Cu and I co-localize where crystals form, while carbon remains uniform
evidence_result.evidence_span: The composite EDX elemental map [Fig. 5(c)] shows copper (Cu) and iodine (I) co-localized in the regions where crystals have formed, while the carbon (C) signal remains uniform across the graphene template.

evidence_result.content: Crystal-free regions have much lower Cu and I signal than crystal-covered regions
evidence_result.evidence_span: In the crystal-free region [region 1 in Fig. 5(c)] the Cu and I fractions fall to 0.38 and 0.05 at%, that is, 18 and 102 times below the crystal-covered region.

evidence_result.content: Measured Cu:I ratio is consistent with CuI stoichiometry
evidence_result.evidence_span: The resulting Cu:I ratio of 1.4 ± 0.3 is consistent with the 1:1 stoichiometry of copper(I) iodide within the accuracy of standardless EDX quantification.

evidence_result.content: S and Na were below detection, implying SDS removal and a clean template
evidence_result.evidence_span: Sulfur (from the SDS surfactant) and sodium were not detected within the signal-to-noise limits of the current EDX acquisition. This suggests an efficient removal of SDS surfactant used during the DSA process to form the continuous oxo-G film.

evidence_result.content: DFT finds h-CuI on SLG less favorable than bulk γ-CuI, but encapsulation would stabilize it
evidence_result.evidence_span: Thus, the h-CuI monolayer on SLG is energetically about 7.0 meV/Å2 less favorable than γ-CuI. A graphene-encapsulated h-CuI monolayer would be more favorable than γ-CuI by 6.6 meV/Å2.

evidence_result.content: A tested graphene defect changes adhesion negligibly, so the energy balance is essentially unchanged
evidence_result.evidence_span: DFT calculations for a defective graphene substrate (Methods) give an adhesion of 13.65 meV/Å2, only 0.5% above the pristine value of 13.58 meV/Å2; the single defective configuration examined therefore leaves the balance of Eq. (1) unchanged.

evidence_result.content: Adding a realistic adlayer spacing cuts recovered adhesion to only 10–17% of the original
evidence_result.evidence_span: Inserting Δz = 2.8–3.7 Å into Eq. (2) leaves a recovered adhesion of only 1.4–2.3 meV/Å2, that is 10–17% of E0

evidence_result.content: At 180 °C, coalesced domains and cleaner EDX signatures are observed
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 180 °C, coalesced domains form (Fig. 3; Fig. 5), and STEM-EDX records a cleaner interface, with the oxygen signal dropping and sulfur and sodium falling below the detection limit (Fig. S1).

evidence_result.content: AIMD shows characteristic hexagonal PDF peaks retained at 300 K on SLG and in BLG
evidence_result.evidence_span: The characteristic maxima in the distribution functions show that the hexagonal lattice is retained at 300 K both on SLG and within BLG.

evidence_result.content: At 600 K iodine remains localized while Cu becomes more dynamic
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 600 K the iodine atoms remain strongly localized, while the Cu atoms show increased dynamics.

evidence_result.content: AIMD indicates 2D h-CuI stays dynamically stable on open graphene and when encapsulated at 300 and 600 K
evidence_result.evidence_span: The trajectories show that 2D h-CuI remains dynamically stable not only within a graphene sandwich but also on an open graphene surface at both 300 and 600 K.

evidence_result.content: Using an Au grid instead of Cu produced no h-CuI crystals
evidence_result.evidence_span: Under these conditions, no h-CuI crystals were observed.

evidence_result.content: Bright particles on holey carbon are identified as residual gold contamination by EDX
evidence_result.evidence_span: In HAADF-STEM images of HI-treated and annealed samples, bright high-contrast particles are observed mainly on the holey-carbon support; EDX identifies them as residual gold contamination.

evidence_result.content: Measured anisotropy of annealed aligned crystallites matches the laterally free uniaxial prediction, not the constrained one
evidence_result.evidence_span: The measured lattice anisotropy of the two annealed, graphene-aligned crystallites, 1.017 ± 0.004 (Sample 4) and 1.019 ± 0.004 (Sample 5, Table S1), matches the laterally free prediction of 1.018 rather than the laterally constrained value of 1.012

evidence_result.content: Sample 5 shows contraction below aCuI, confirming perpendicular Poisson contraction
evidence_result.evidence_span: The contraction seen in Sample 5 (b ≈ 4.18 Å < aCuI = 4.19 Å, Table S1) confirms the perpendicular Poisson contraction.

evidence_result.content: Direct DFT gives nearly identical adhesion for pristine and defective graphene
evidence_result.evidence_span: The calculated values are 13.58 meV/Å2 (0.218 J/m2) for pristine graphene and 13.65 meV/Å2 for defective graphene.

evidence_result.content: One graphene interface lowers but does not eliminate the h-CuI metastability relative to bulk γ-CuI, while two interfaces make it favorable
evidence_result.evidence_span: One graphene interface (13.58 meV/Å2) reduces the energy difference of h-CuI and bulk γ-CuI, however leaving the h-CuI/SLG heterostructure still about +7.0 meV/Å2 above γ (metastable, kinetically trapped); a second interface further reduces the energy difference to −6.6 meV/Å2 (thermodynamically favored).

evidence_result.content: Adding an extra interfacial gap of 2.8–3.7 Å reduces adhesion to 2.3 or 1.4 meV/Å², i.e. 17% or 10% of the original
evidence_result.evidence_span: Evaluating EvdW(z0 + Δz) for an additional gap Δz = 2.8–3.7 Å gives 2.3 meV/Å2 at Δz = 2.8 Å and 1.4 meV/Å2 at Δz = 3.7 Å, that is 17% and 10% of E0.

evidence_result.content: Iodine displacement plateaus in both directions within segments, while copper in-plane displacement keeps increasing
evidence_result.evidence_span: Within these segments the iodine displacement reaches a plateau in both directions, while the copper in-plane displacement continues to rise.

constraint.content: Observed uniaxial strain constrains the corrugation energy to lie between uniaxial and biaxial strain costs
constraint.evidence_span: The corrugation gain must therefore exceed the uniaxial cost but stay below the biaxial one, 0.30 < ΔUP,eff < 1.05 meV/Å2.

constraint.content: Once interface is clean, growth is mainly limited by precursor supply to the graphene–CuI interface
constraint.evidence_span: Where the interface is clean, further growth is expected to be limited mainly by precursor supply to the graphene–CuI interface.

constraint.content: The layer must accommodate the in-plane lattice mismatch as strain
constraint.evidence_span: The experimental in-plane lattice mismatch is δ ≈ 1.67% (aCuI = 4.19 Å, √3·aG = 4.26 Å, see Table S3), and the layer must take it up as a strain ε = δ.

constraint.content: A frequency is only resolved if every contributing segment contains at least one full oscillation period
constraint.evidence_span: In Fig. 6 of the main paper, a frequency is resolved in a segment-averaged spectrum only if every contributing segment holds at least one full period of it.

constraint.content: Dynamics beyond the ~1.5 ps restart segments cannot be accessed by these trajectories
constraint.evidence_span: Time scales beyond the restart segments are outside the reach of these trajectories.

contradiction.content: Unlike prior encapsulated h-CuI reports, open monolayer h-CuI shows no perpendicular contraction
contradiction.evidence_span: In our open monolayer the perpendicular direction is not contracted below the intrinsic h-CuI value, i.e. the uniaxial adaptation proceeds without a perpendicular (Poisson) compression, whereas Mustonen et al. [26] report a comparable anisotropy for graphene-encapsulated 2D h-CuI.

contradiction.content: Experimentally inferred corrugation lower bound exceeds prior DFT literature values
contradiction.evidence_span: The lower bound inferred from the observed uniaxial strain exceeds the corrugation amplitudes reported from DFT calculations in the literature (≤ 0.14 meV/Å2, Table S3) [28] by about a factor of two

problem_motivation.content: To explain why wet-chemical growth does not yield h-CuI on open monolayer graphene regions.
evidence_spans: it offers an explanation for the absence of h-CuI on open monolayer regions in the wet-chemical route [26].

prior_approach.content: Prior simulations considered freestanding and encapsulated 2D h-CuI, including Ullah et al.'s study of encapsulated CuI/graphene where registry-dependent stacking energy was computed by sliding and rotating the layers across five configurations, but they had not yet addressed open-substrate supported 2D h-CuI on graphene.
evidence_spans: Published calculations thus considered the freestanding monolayer [17,23] and the encapsulated layer [26,28] but not yet 2D h-CuI on an open graphene substrate

The upper bound of this range is derived from Ullah et al. [S11], who computed the registry-dependent stacking energy of CuI encapsulated by graphene by sliding and rotating the layers across five distinct configurations and found the total energy variation to be < 0.3 meV/atom

rejected_alternative.content: The γ-CuI growth route is rejected because it depends on a high-temperature CuI vapor/molecular CuI flux used in prior γ-CuI nanosheet and epitaxial film growth, whereas in this process no component exceeds 180 °C, so appreciable CuI sublimation and the required flux are absent.
evidence_spans: routes that yield γ-CuI nanosheets and epitaxial γ-CuI films sublime CuI powder from sources held at 360–450 °C [24,25]; in our process no component exceeds 180 °C, far below appreciable CuI sublimation, so the molecular CuI flux that enables γ-phase growth is absent.

rejected_alternative.content: Multilayer h-CuI/β-CuI formation is rejected as unlikely because h-CuI basal planes are self-saturating and lack dangling bonds, so they cannot template γ-CuI, and because Cu and I precursors are delivered on graphene rather than on top of h-CuI, preventing second-layer nucleation.
evidence_spans: Second, the h-CuI surface is self-saturating: its basal planes carry no dangling bonds, so the iodine-terminated basal h-CuI plane cannot template γ-CuI. Moreover, the precursor species Cu and I are supplied on graphene and not on top of h-CuI, so a second layer cannot nucleate, which makes multilayer h-CuI (β-CuI) equally unlikely.

inspiration_source.content: The film compression/deposition method was inspired by and modeled after the Langmuir–Blodgett process, differing in that SDS molecules rearranged by self-assembly to maintain a compact, uniform monolayer during deposition.
evidence_spans: The compression was analogous to the Langmuir–Blodgett process, with the difference that the SDS molecules rearranged by self-assembly, so that a compact, uniform monolayer was maintained throughout the deposition.

causal_claim.content: HI vapor serves a dual role in the synthesis: it reduces oxo-graphene to reduced oxo-graphene and attacks/etches the Cu TEM grid, supplying copper; together with iodine from HI, this initiates nucleation of small h-CuI crystallites.
evidence_spans: where HI serves a dual purpose: it reduces the oxo-G to reduced oxo-graphene (r-oxo-G) [30], and it attacks the copper of the grid, the solid-state copper source of the synthesis.
This treatment reduces the oxo-G and simultaneously initiates the nucleation of small h-CuI crystallites, formed from iodine supplied by the reducing agent and copper provided by the TEM grid.

causal_claim.content: The Cu TEM grid is the sole copper source for h-CuI formation; the absence of h-CuI on Au confirms this solid-state precursor origin.
evidence_spans: The absence of h-CuI formation on the Au grid confirms that the copper from the Cu TEM grid is the sole source of Cu atoms in our synthesis, validating the solid-state precursor approach.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing at 180 °C promotes the iodine-copper reaction and further growth of initially formed/intercalated h-CuI crystallites into extended, well-defined van der Waals-epitaxial domains, while significantly improving crystallinity and promoting lattice relaxation.
evidence_spans: In the second step, annealing at 180 °C grows the crystallites into extended, van der Waals-epitaxial domains.
Thermal annealing at 180 °C significantly improves crystallinity and promotes lattice relaxation.
Thermal annealing at 180 °C promotes the further growth of these intercalated domains [Fig. 4(d)].

Finally, the sample undergoes thermal annealing at 180 °C, which promotes the reaction between iodine and copper to form extended, well-defined h-CuI crystals on the reduced oxo-G (r-oxo-G) substrate or sandwiched between the graphene nanosheets of bilayer r-oxo-G.

causal_claim.content: Thermal annealing reduces the oxygen signal, indicating effective removal of oxygen-containing functional groups and adsorbed water from the initial oxo-G template.
evidence_spans: Thermal annealing significantly reduces the oxygen signal in the EDX maps (see Fig. S1e), indicating the effective removal of oxygen-containing functional groups and adsorbed water from the initial oxo-G template during the HI treatment and subsequent annealing.

causal_claim.content: Because Cu and I precursors arrive separately at the graphene interface, CuI forms in situ under dilute conditions, making the local supersaturation needed for 3D γ-CuI nucleation unlikely.
evidence_spans: Thus, CuI forms in situ under dilute conditions, and the local supersaturation required to nucleate a three-dimensional γ-CuI particle is unlikely to be reached.

causal_claim.content: Intercalation growth in twisted bilayer graphene proceeds analogously to open monolayer growth, with h-CuI growing epitaxially with a hexagonal lattice in both cases.
evidence_spans: In both, h-CuI grows epitaxially with a hexagonal lattice, which shows that intercalation into twisted bilayer graphene proceeds analogously to growth on the open monolayer surface.

causal_claim.content: Interfacial adlayers/adsorbates strongly weaken adhesion and reduce the van der Waals stabilization needed for supported h-CuI epitaxial growth; where adsorbates remain, adhesion recovery does not occur and growth stops.
evidence_spans: In contrast, interfacial adlayers have a pronounced effect on the epitaxial growth.
where adsorbates remain on the surface, the adhesion term of Eq. (1) is not recovered and growth stops.
Such an interfacial layer therefore strongly reduces the van der Waals stabilization required for growth of supported h-CuI.

causal_claim.content: A stiffer graphene environment constrains and suppresses relaxation/motion of h-CuI: the graphene substrate suppresses lateral relaxation of soft h-CuI, making the laterally constrained uniaxial estimate applicable; a single graphene layer damps relative out-of-plane h-CuI motion by about an order of magnitude, and a second graphene interface stiffens the in-plane transverse optical mode.
evidence_spans: This laterally constrained form (εyy ≈ 0) is the upper estimate of the uniaxial strain cost, applicable when the stiffer graphene substrate (E2DGr ≈ 340 N/m) suppresses lateral relaxation of the soft h-CuI (E2D ≈ 35 N/m, Table S3).
Thus, a single graphene layer damps the relative out-of-plane movement of h-CuI between 1.20 and 1.55 THz by an order of magnitude in normalized power.
For this collective in-plane movement, a second interface stiffens the h-CuI sheet.

causal_claim.content: Supported h-CuI follows the out-of-plane motion of its graphene layer more closely than encapsulated h-CuI pairs do.
evidence_spans: The supported h-CuI sheet follows the out-of-plane motion of its graphene layer more closely than either pair of the encapsulated cell.

mechanism_principle.content: Cu released from the support grid diffuses across graphene at room temperature and reacts with iodine adsorbed during HI treatment, causing nucleation of small hexagonal CuI crystallites.
evidence_spans: The copper released from the grid crosses the graphene by surface diffusion, on a potential energy landscape flat enough for copper adatoms to migrate anomalously at room temperature [32], and meets the iodine adsorbed during the HI treatment, where small hexagonal CuI (h-CuI) crystallites nucleate.

mechanism_principle.content: The preferred 30° epitaxial offset of h-CuI on graphene arises because the energetically favored registry places iodine atoms at the centers of graphene hexagons; this hexagon-center sublattice is rotated by 30° relative to the graphene atomic lattice.
evidence_spans: Physically, the 30° offset reflects the energetically preferred registry in which the iodine atoms occupy the centers of the graphene hexagons [26]; this hexagon-center sublattice is rotated by 30° relative to the graphene atomic lattice, so θ = 0 corresponds to perfect epitaxial lock-in (Section S2c).

mechanism_principle.content: Near-isotropy of small bilayer h-CuI nuclei is attributed to their early growth stage: because the nuclei are small and have a high edge-to-area ratio, they have not yet developed the directional lattice adaptation seen in larger domains.
evidence_spans: We attribute the near-absence of in-plane anisotropy to the early stage of growth: the nucleus is small and has a high edge-to-area ratio, so its lattice has not yet developed the directional adaptation that characterizes larger, fully grown domains.

mechanism_principle.content: Different registry relationships with the two graphene sheets show that h-CuI is encapsulated between graphene layers rather than sitting on the outer bilayer surface, since an outer-surface crystallite would be templated only by the outermost sheet in both cases.
evidence_spans: A crystallite on an outer surface of bilayer graphene would be templated by the outermost sheet in both cases, so registry with different graphene layers would be impossible. Both crystals are shown together in one image in Fig. S2, identifying the h-CuI as encapsulated within two graphene sheets (Section S3).

mechanism_principle.content: Formation of hexagonal CuI does not require it to be thermodynamically more stable than bulk γ-CuI; rather, under HI-treatment conditions, the nucleation pathway/conditions needed for γ-CuI never occur.
evidence_spans: Under these conditions where HI functions as both the reducing agent and the iodine source, the hexagonal phase does not have to be thermodynamically more favorable than γ-CuI. The conditions under which γ-CuI nucleates do not arise in the first place.

mechanism_principle.content: Previous DFT likely underestimated adhesion/binding because of simplifications in the assumed van der Waals potential; moreover, adhesion falls steeply with increasing interlayer gap due to the z^-4 tail of the planar vdW potential, so reduced adhesion cannot compensate the metastability penalty of 2D h-CuI relative to bulk γ-CuI.
evidence_spans: which we ascribe to the unavoidable simplification in the vdW potential assumed in those calculations.
which cannot compensate the 20.5 meV/Å2 by which the 2D phase lies above bulk γ-CuI.
The adhesion decays steeply due to the z −4 tail.

mechanism_principle.content: In bilayer graphene, van der Waals pressure expels some adsorbates into pockets and presses the sheets together where adsorbates are absent, improving binding; correspondingly, residual oxo-groups, water, and iodine limit h-CuI crystal size, while larger domains occur where adsorbates are removed and the interface is locally cleaner.
evidence_spans: Within a bilayer, the van der Waals pressure expels part of the adsorbates into pockets [42,43] and presses the layers together, supporting the binding where adsorbates cannot be removed.
After the 40 °C HI treatment the reduced oxo-graphene surface still carries residual oxo-groups, physisorbed water, and adsorbed iodine [35], limiting the size of the h-CuI crystallites.

This correlation is consistent with a contribution from adsorbate removal; ... The lateral domain size therefore correlates with the local cleanliness of the interface, as seen in Fig. S2, where the h-CuI crystals extend up to the next adsorbate on the surface.

mechanism_principle.content: Graphene acts as a van der Waals spring that damps out-of-plane motion of the nearby iodine sublayer, a mechanism linked to the experimentally observed preference for uniaxial rather than isotropic strain adaptation, consistent with the large strain anisotropy factor.
evidence_spans: The vdW spring of graphene thus damps the out-of-plane movement of the iodine sublayer in its vicinity.
This anisotropy factor [Eq. (S8)] helps explain the preference for uniaxial adaptation observed experimentally.

hypothesis_statement.content: Oxo-G retains sufficient lattice periodicity to serve as a robust template for van der Waals epitaxy.
evidence_spans: These well-defined crystallographic signatures demonstrate that the oxo-G retains the lattice periodicity required to act as a robust template for van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy.

hypothesis_statement.content: Formation-energy estimates indicate that h-CuI is metastable.
evidence_spans: An estimate of the formation energies indicates that h-CuI is metastable.

evidence_result.content: Control experiments on gold TEM grids produced no h-CuI under otherwise identical conditions, showing that the copper in h-CuI originates from the copper grid rather than the treatment itself.
evidence_spans: The copper originates solely from the grid: a control synthesis on a gold (Au) TEM grid, under otherwise identical conditions, yields no h-CuI (Supporting Information, Section S1).
Under these conditions, no h-CuI crystals were observed.

evidence_result.content: HI treatment alone nucleates discrete ~5 nm h-CuI crystallites on monolayer and bilayer graphene; in the bilayer-intercalated early stage these nuclei are nearly isotropic.
evidence_spans: HRTEM imaging revealed the nucleation of discrete h-CuI crystallites of about 5 nm on monolayer and bilayer r-oxo-G.
These values correspond to an essentially isotropic crystallite.

evidence_result.content: After annealing, h-CuI domains become larger/coalesced and diffraction spots sharpen; at 180 °C STEM-EDX also indicates a cleaner interface, with reduced oxygen and sulfur/sodium below detection.
evidence_spans: Post-annealing HRTEM imaging [Fig. 3(d)] reveals increased domain sizes and sharper diffraction spots [Fig. 3(e)]
At 180 °C, coalesced domains form (Fig. 3; Fig. 5), and STEM-EDX records a cleaner interface, with the oxygen signal dropping and sulfur and sodium falling below the detection limit (Fig. S1).

evidence_result.content: Annealed bilayer h-CuI shows uniaxial epitaxial adaptation to graphene: one in-plane direction becomes commensurate with the graphene template while the perpendicular direction remains close to the intrinsic h-CuI spacing, yielding about 1.7% anisotropy consistent with the laterally free uniaxial-strain prediction rather than the constrained case; Sample 5 additionally shows perpendicular Poisson contraction below a_CuI.
evidence_spans: The adaptation is uniaxial: along one direction an h-CuI vector matches the substrate period, while the perpendicular vector stays close to the intrinsic h-CuI value and retains a residual mismatch of about 1.4% (from the initial 1.67% lattice mismatch).

The anisotropy of 1.7% indicates the uniaxial strain profile, reflecting the lattice adaptation to the epitaxial template in only one direction, while h-CuI remains relaxed in the perpendicular direction, where b1 = 0.419 ± 0.002 nm is close to the intrinsic value.

The measured lattice anisotropy of the two annealed, graphene-aligned crystallites, 1.017 ± 0.004 (Sample 4) and 1.019 ± 0.004 (Sample 5, Table S1), matches the laterally free prediction of 1.018 rather than the laterally constrained value of 1.012
The contraction seen in Sample 5 (b ≈ 4.18 Å < aCuI = 4.19 Å, Table S1) confirms the perpendicular Poisson contraction.

evidence_result.content: STEM-EDX shows Cu and I co-localize where crystals form while carbon stays uniform; crystal-free regions contain far less Cu and I than crystal-covered regions; the measured Cu:I ratio (1.4 ± 0.3) is consistent with CuI stoichiometry.
evidence_spans: The composite EDX elemental map [Fig. 5(c)] shows copper (Cu) and iodine (I) co-localized in the regions where crystals have formed, while the carbon (C) signal remains uniform across the graphene template.
In the crystal-free region [region 1 in Fig. 5(c)] the Cu and I fractions fall to 0.38 and 0.05 at%, that is, 18 and 102 times below the crystal-covered region.
The resulting Cu:I ratio of 1.4 ± 0.3 is consistent with the 1:1 stoichiometry of copper(I) iodide within the accuracy of standardless EDX quantification.

evidence_result.content: EDX did not detect sulfur or sodium, implying efficient removal of SDS surfactant and a clean graphene template/interface after processing.
evidence_spans: Sulfur (from the SDS surfactant) and sodium were not detected within the signal-to-noise limits of the current EDX acquisition. This suggests an efficient removal of SDS surfactant used during the DSA process to form the continuous oxo-G film.
At 180 °C, coalesced domains form (Fig. 3; Fig. 5), and STEM-EDX records a cleaner interface, with the oxygen signal dropping and sulfur and sodium falling below the detection limit (Fig. S1).

evidence_result.content: Bright high-contrast particles seen mainly on the holey-carbon support are residual gold contamination, as identified by EDX, rather than h-CuI.
evidence_spans: In HAADF-STEM images of HI-treated and annealed samples, bright high-contrast particles are observed mainly on the holey-carbon support; EDX identifies them as residual gold contamination.

evidence_result.content: DFT indicates that h-CuI on single-layer graphene is still metastable relative to bulk γ-CuI by about +7.0 meV/Å², but graphene encapsulation (two interfaces) stabilizes h-CuI and makes it favorable by about −6.6 meV/Å².
evidence_spans: Thus, the h-CuI monolayer on SLG is energetically about 7.0 meV/Å2 less favorable than γ-CuI. A graphene-encapsulated h-CuI monolayer would be more favorable than γ-CuI by 6.6 meV/Å2.

One graphene interface (13.58 meV/Å2) reduces the energy difference of h-CuI and bulk γ-CuI, however leaving the h-CuI/SLG heterostructure still about +7.0 meV/Å2 above γ (metastable, kinetically trapped); a second interface further reduces the energy difference to −6.6 meV/Å2 (thermodynamically favored).

evidence_result.content: Direct DFT gives nearly identical adhesion energies for pristine and the tested defective graphene, so that defect has negligible effect on the h-CuI/graphene energy balance.
evidence_spans: DFT calculations for a defective graphene substrate (Methods) give an adhesion of 13.65 meV/Å2, only 0.5% above the pristine value of 13.58 meV/Å2; the single defective configuration examined therefore leaves the balance of Eq. (1) unchanged.
The calculated values are 13.58 meV/Å2 (0.218 J/m2) for pristine graphene and 13.65 meV/Å2 for defective graphene.

evidence_result.content: Introducing a realistic extra interfacial gap of 2.8–3.7 Å drastically reduces the recovered van der Waals adhesion to about 2.3–1.4 meV/Å², i.e. only 17–10% of the original adhesion.
evidence_spans: Inserting Δz = 2.8–3.7 Å into Eq. (2) leaves a recovered adhesion of only 1.4–2.3 meV/Å2, that is 10–17% of E0
Evaluating EvdW(z0 + Δz) for an additional gap Δz = 2.8–3.7 Å gives 2.3 meV/Å2 at Δz = 2.8 Å and 1.4 meV/Å2 at Δz = 3.7 Å, that is 17% and 10% of E0.

evidence_result.content: AIMD shows that 2D h-CuI remains dynamically stable on single-layer graphene and within bilayer graphene/graphene encapsulation at both 300 K and 600 K; the hexagonal lattice is retained at 300 K, while at 600 K iodine remains localized and its displacement plateaus whereas copper becomes more dynamic, with in-plane displacement continuing to increase.
evidence_spans: The characteristic maxima in the distribution functions show that the hexagonal lattice is retained at 300 K both on SLG and within BLG.
At 600 K the iodine atoms remain strongly localized, while the Cu atoms show increased dynamics.
The trajectories show that 2D h-CuI remains dynamically stable not only within a graphene sandwich but also on an open graphene surface at both 300 and 600 K.
Within these segments the iodine displacement reaches a plateau in both directions, while the copper in-plane displacement continues to rise.

constraint.content: Observed uniaxial strain constrains the corrugation energy to lie between the uniaxial and biaxial strain costs, specifically 0.30 < ΔU_P,eff < 1.05 meV/Å².
evidence_spans: The corrugation gain must therefore exceed the uniaxial cost but stay below the biaxial one, 0.30 < ΔUP,eff < 1.05 meV/Å2.

constraint.content: The layer must accommodate the experimental in-plane lattice mismatch as strain, with ε = δ ≈ 1.67% (from a_CuI = 4.19 Å and √3·a_G = 4.26 Å).
evidence_spans: The experimental in-plane lattice mismatch is δ ≈ 1.67% (aCuI = 4.19 Å, √3·aG = 4.26 Å, see Table S3), and the layer must take it up as a strain ε = δ.

constraint.content: Where the interface is clean, further growth is constrained mainly by precursor supply to the graphene–CuI interface.
evidence_spans: Where the interface is clean, further growth is expected to be limited mainly by precursor supply to the graphene–CuI interface.

constraint.content: In segment-averaged spectra, a frequency is resolved only if every contributing segment contains at least one full oscillation period of that frequency.
evidence_spans: In Fig. 6 of the main paper, a frequency is resolved in a segment-averaged spectrum only if every contributing segment holds at least one full period of it.

constraint.content: These trajectories cannot access dynamics on time scales longer than the ~1.5 ps restart segments.
evidence_spans: Time scales beyond the restart segments are outside the reach of these trajectories.

contradiction.content: Open monolayer h-CuI behaves differently from prior graphene-encapsulated h-CuI reports: it shows no perpendicular (Poisson) contraction below the intrinsic h-CuI value during uniaxial adaptation, unlike the comparable anisotropy reported by Mustonen et al. for encapsulated 2D h-CuI.
evidence_spans: In our open monolayer the perpendicular direction is not contracted below the intrinsic h-CuI value, i.e. the uniaxial adaptation proceeds without a perpendicular (Poisson) compression, whereas Mustonen et al. [26] report a comparable anisotropy for graphene-encapsulated 2D h-CuI.

contradiction.content: The experimentally inferred lower bound on corrugation is substantially larger than prior DFT literature values, exceeding reported corrugation amplitudes (≤ 0.14 meV/Å2) by about a factor of two.
evidence_spans: The lower bound inferred from the observed uniaxial strain exceeds the corrugation amplitudes reported from DFT calculations in the literature (≤ 0.14 meV/Å2, Table S3) [28] by about a factor of two
